title: John Hersey and the horrors of Hiroshima
gist: New START expired in February 2026 with nothing to replace it, removing the last legal limit on the two largest nuclear arsenals just as China's stockpile more than doubled in five years, Iran debates NPT withdrawal openly, and Poland, Turkey and South Korea drift toward domestic nuclear capability — which is why MacGregor revisits John Hersey's 1946 New Yorker 'Hiroshima', the article that occupied an entire issue, sold out by midday, hit 250,000 book copies in a week and, on Hersey's own later account, made memory rather than deterrence the thing that has kept the world safe.

insights.claim: New START, enforced since 2011 and the last remaining arms-control agreement between the United States and Russia, expired in February 2026 with nothing to replace it, removing the final legal barrier limiting the world's two largest nuclear arsenals.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: An unconstrained US-Russia arsenal is a structurally new tail risk regime for 2026 onward — relevant to defence budgets and long-dated geopolitical risk premia.
insights.locator: The New START treaty – enforced since 2011

insights.claim: China is rapidly expanding and modernising its nuclear forces, with its stockpile more than doubling in just five years and further growth expected throughout the decade.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A three-way arsenal race replaces the bilateral model that all Cold War stability doctrine was built on.
insights.locator: China, meanwhile, is rapidly expanding

insights.claim: Recent US-Israeli attacks have pushed Iran closer than ever to abandoning the NPT, with Tehran still holding enough enriched uranium for short technical reach to multiple warheads and senior figures openly debating withdrawal as a defensive necessity rather than a diplomatic taboo.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Military strikes have raised, not lowered, the probability of Iranian breakout — a direct input to Gulf energy and shipping risk.
insights.locator: In the Middle East, the erosion of nuclear restraint

insights.claim: A major regional power crossing the nuclear threshold outside any arms-control framework would set a precedent reverberating far beyond the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Iranian breakout should be modelled as a cascade trigger, not a contained regional event.
insights.locator: The precedent – of a major regional power

insights.claim: Public opinion in Poland, Turkey and South Korea is shifting toward domestic nuclear capability as confidence in US security guarantees frays, while North Korea insists its arsenal is 'irreversible'.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Alliance credibility is now the load-bearing variable for non-proliferation; three US allies are candidate proliferators.
insights.locator: North Korea, emboldened by global fragmentation

insights.claim: The precarious equilibrium of the non-proliferation era is cracking precisely when living memory of the bomb's human cost has never been more vital.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: The author's core argument: the restraint mechanism is cultural memory, and it is decaying at the same time as the legal one.
insights.locator: The precarious equilibrium of the non-proliferation era

insights.claim: Hersey was born in 1914 in the treaty port of Tientsin to American missionary parents and spoke Mandarin before English, absorbing the stoicism and endurance of Chinese families — the first training of an observer who spent his life listening to those the world overlooked.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Cross-cultural formation, not credentials, produced the access and register that made the Hiroshima reporting possible.
insights.locator: The story of John Hersey begins far from the editorial offices

insights.claim: Henry Luce recruited Hersey to Time partly because Luce had himself been shaped by a childhood in China a generation earlier and recognised a familiar sensibility, sending him back to Asia almost immediately.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Editorial gatekeepers select for their own biography — a structural reason certain stories get commissioned and others do not.
insights.locator: In 1937 he returned to the United States

insights.claim: As Time's Chungking correspondent from 1939, Hersey's fluency in Mandarin opened doors other Western correspondents never approached, giving him access to bombed neighbourhoods, ministries, refugee camps and Japanese blockades.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Language capability is the underrated determinant of reporting quality in foreign conflict coverage.
insights.locator: As Hersey’s papers tell us, Luce sent him back

insights.claim: Hersey's method was radical proximity: he insisted on going where soldiers went, sleeping where they slept and eating what they ate, living on Guadalcanal in 1942 in a foxhole that was once a hut.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: The credibility of the later Hiroshima piece rested on years of accumulated field authority — trust is built before it is spent.
insights.quote: ‘my bedroom was the hollow empty sky, and every once in a while, a 105mm shell would scream in one window and out the other’
insights.locator: Covering the bitter fighting on Guadalcanal in 1942

insights.claim: When Hersey asked Marines what they were fighting for, they answered roast beef, pies and kitchens back home — a line that cut straight through the mythologising of war.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Asking the concrete question rather than the ideological one is the technique that produces non-propagandistic evidence.
insights.quote: ‘Home is what they talk about on Guadal’
insights.locator: He asked them: ‘Today here in this valley

insights.claim: By 1945 Hersey had survived four air crashes, protected his notebooks by sealing them in condoms in tropical rain, published Into the Valley (1943) and won the 1944 Pulitzer Prize for A Bell for Adano.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Establishes the pre-existing reputational capital that let a single magazine article move national opinion.
insights.locator: His notebooks were sacrosanct

insights.claim: The structure of 'Hiroshima' came from a chance shipboard reading of Thornton Wilder's The Bridge of San Luis Rey while Hersey lay feverish with flu — five lives intertwined by a single moment of catastrophe became the blueprint for tracking a small selection of lives through the bomb.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
entities: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
insights.so_what: The narrative container, borrowed from fiction, was what made incomprehensible scale legible — a transferable communication technique.
insights.locator: Before he could begin, Hersey had to reach Japan

insights.claim: Hersey built the piece around six named survivors — Hatsuyo Nakamura, Toshiko Sasaki, Father Wilhelm Kleinsorge, Dr Terufumi Sasaki, Dr Masakazu Fujii and pastor Kiyoshi Tanimoto — tracing where each stood at 8:15 am to restore proportion rather than convey megatonnage.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Six verifiable individuals defeated an official narrative that aggregate statistics never could.
insights.locator: Slowly he found the figures who would shape his narrative

insights.claim: The article's power lay in its restraint: Hersey neither condemned nor defended the bombing, he merely described what happened to six people, and that was enough to unsettle a world.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Withholding argument can be more persuasive than making one — a durable lesson about how contested evidence is best delivered.
insights.quote: Its power lay in its restraint.
insights.locator: Yet none of these critiques endured

insights.claim: Under MacArthur's Press Code, Japanese newspapers could not mention radiation, long-term burns, acute sickness or starvation, so the atomic bomb was discussed publicly as an event of physics and strategy rather than of bodies and pain.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Occupying powers control the vocabulary available to describe their own actions — the mechanism by which official narratives persist.
insights.locator: Under MacArthur’s command, a strict Press Code

insights.claim: MacArthur's censors did not understand what Hersey was doing because foreign correspondents were less scrutinised than Japanese reporters and his questions were quiet, humane and seemingly apolitical.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Censorship regimes filter on tone and topic keywords, so unaggressive method is the reliable route past them.
insights.locator: Crucially, MacArthur’s censors did not understand

insights.claim: The article was cleared by General Leslie Groves, who believed Hersey's apocalyptic narrative would support his own argument that the US must arm itself against anyone else developing the weapon — even though he had spent months publicly downplaying radiation deaths.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: The censor approved the piece for instrumental reasons and misjudged it entirely — a case study in how gatekeepers misread the effect of what they release.
insights.locator: It still had to pass official censorship

insights.claim: Occupation Japan was in reality an American governorship with some 430,000 US troops on the Home Islands by late 1945 living 'in almost neocolonial fashion', supplied plentifully while Japanese civilians queued for rations among ruins.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: The material asymmetry of occupation is the backdrop that made the survivors' testimony politically explosive.
insights.locator: The now-defeated country he stepped into

insights.claim: The New Yorker devoted an entire issue to a single article for the first time in its history when 'A Noiseless Flash' appeared on 31 August 1946, its ordinary Central Park cover and deceptively blank contents page concealing all 47 pages of one story.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Format itself carried the message — an editorial gamble with no precedent and no fallback.
insights.quote: It felt less like a magazine than a memorial printed in black ink.
insights.locator: When ‘A Noiseless Flash’ appeared in the New Yorker

insights.claim: Diffusion was near-instantaneous and cross-media: the issue sold out on New York newsstands by midday, Harvard students queued at the bookstore, priests read it from pulpits, and an NBC announcer read it live on air until the station closed at midnight, with radio stations nationwide following.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A single well-formed artefact can saturate a national information environment within 24 hours — the pre-internet template for virality.
insights.locator: In the first hours of publication

insights.claim: The New York Times came as close as it had to questioning the bomb's rationale, editorialising that one may think the bombing sound recalling Tarawa, Iwo Jima or Okinawa, and unsound when reading Hersey.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Elite media reframing of a settled national consensus, achieved by evidence rather than argument.
insights.quote: ‘One may think [the bombing] sound when he recalls Tarawa, Iwo Jima, or Okinawa. One may think it unsound when he reads Mr Hersey.’
insights.locator: The New York Times, in a now-famous editorial

insights.claim: Albert Einstein publicly declared he had purchased a thousand copies of the New Yorker to send to science facilities and physicists, amplifying the wave of opinion that recognised the dangers Hersey described.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Scientific-elite endorsement converted public shock into an organised movement — the mechanism by which reporting becomes policy pressure.
insights.locator: Albert Einstein had been long convinced

insights.claim: The book edition sold 250,000 copies in a single week, a record for its time, while the BBC produced an unprecedented full radio dramatisation, French, Italian and Dutch papers reprinted whole sections despite acute paper shortages, and Scandinavian schools adopted it as a set text within months.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Quantified evidence of how fast a moral narrative can globalise even under postwar material constraints.
insights.locator: The international reaction was even more dramatic

insights.claim: Clandestine translations circulated in Japan within days, passed hand to hand among survivors who for a year had lived under a system in which their medical suffering could not be named publicly.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Censorship failed at the point where the censored population itself became the distribution network.
insights.locator: Within days, clandestine translations of ‘Hiroshima’

insights.claim: Groves was appalled because Hersey's calmly precise descriptions of burns, fevers, missing skin, infections, hair loss and maggot-infested wounds contradicted his standing insistence that radiation sickness was exaggerated or temporary — but he could not refute the facts because the six survivors were real.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Named, documented individuals are the format official denial cannot absorb — the durable lesson for contested-evidence disputes.
insights.locator: General Groves was appalled at the public reaction

insights.claim: Critics on the American right called the article unpatriotic and some military officials accused Hersey of giving 'aid and comfort to the enemy' though the war was already over, yet none of these critiques endured.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Loyalty-based attacks on verified reporting have a short half-life relative to the reporting itself.
insights.locator: Naturally, there was political fallout

insights.claim: Hersey then disappeared from public life — declining interviews, celebratory dinners and invitations to testify — believing he had merely been a courier for voices belonging to the six survivors, and went to teach English literature at Yale.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Refusing to become the story preserved the story's authority — the opposite of the modern attention incentive.
insights.locator: Then something unusual happened

insights.claim: Hersey's own conclusion was that what has kept the world safe from the bomb since 1945 has not been deterrence so much as memory — the memory of what happened at Hiroshima.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: If restraint rests on memory rather than deterrence math, then generational forgetting is itself a proliferation risk factor.
insights.quote: ‘What has kept the world safe from the bomb since 1945’, he wrote later, ‘has not been deterrence… so much as it’s been memory – the memory of what happened at Hiroshima.’
insights.locator: Hersey returned to Hiroshima only once more, in 1985

insights.claim: The Manhattan Project ushered in the atomic age and Truman welcomed the bomb as no different from any conventional weapon; Hersey's words gave that argument a conscience.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: The normalisation of nuclear weapons as ordinary ordnance was an explicit official position that had to be actively defeated — and could return.
insights.quote: ‘I don’t think I’ve ever got as much satisfaction out of anything else in my life.’
insights.locator: The Manhattan Project ushered in the atomic age

insights.claim: Hersey returned to Hiroshima once more in 1985 for 'Hiroshima: The Aftermath', revisiting the six lives four decades later and finding the city rebuilt, the Peace Park established and the survivors aged — but the stories persisting.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Longitudinal follow-up is what converted a piece of journalism into an institution of memory.
insights.locator: Hersey returned to Hiroshima only once more
